newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault, Daewoo sign commercial accord.
newsitem.headline: Renault, Daewoo sign commercial accord.

text.p: French carmaker Renault SA said it had signed a commercial agreement with Daewoo Corp on Thursday to sell engines and engine licences to the Korean company.
It said in a statement that Daewoo would buy 200,000 Renault diesel engines, including a 1.9 litre F8Q engine produced at Cleon, between 1999 and 2002 under the agreement.
Renault will also sell Daewoo four licences to build engines from Renault's range of petrol and diesel engines, including the 1.2 litre D7F engine, for models produced in 2000 and beyond.
Renault did not disclose the terms of the agreement, which was signed on Thursday.
"While enhancing Renault's standing as an engine specialist, the agreement will also provide a substantial amount of additional work for the Cleon factory," the statement said.
"This type of cooperation generates economies of scale, which allow a better amortization of the design and development costs of certain mechanical components," it said.
Renault sells engines and gearboxes to Volvo and Mitsubishi for their NedCar venture in the Netherlands, and it sells automatic transmissions to French car maker PSA Peugeot Citroen.
It signed agreements last year to supply mechanical components to Iran's Kish Khodro and engines to the Russian manufacturer Moskvitch.
"Daewoo will be fitting the diesel engines supplied by Renault to its current vehicles and the engines built under licence will equip cars which are now under development," Renault said.
A Renault spokeswoman said the company declined to give any financial details of the agreement.

Renault, which reported a 5.25 billion franc loss for 1996, has been under pressure from its majority shareholder, the French state with 46 percent, to strike up cooperative accords with other car companies to lower its production costs during a difficult juncture for the European car industry.
The announcement of the agreement came as Renault's unions renewed their protests, calling for a day of action on Friday, against the company's cost-cutting measures.

The measures include plans to shut down the Vilvoorde assembly plant in Belgium that employs 3,100 people, cut nearly 2,800 jobs in France this year and transfer wholly owned dealerships into a separate subsidiary.
The Cleon factory benefitting from the agreement with Daewoo employs 5,470 workers.
